According to Ray Amjad, this approach allows AI agents to autonomously coordinate, delegate tasks and adapt to complex scenarios that previously required extensive human intervention. Explore how multi-agent systems allocate tasks based on complexity, refine processes through iterative feedback and maintain focus on long-term objectives with persistent agents. Gain insight into the operational challenges these systems face, such as managing interdependent goals and minimizing inefficiencies in task distribution. According to a comprehensive scientific review published in npj Sustainable Agriculture by an international research team led by Daoyuan Jin, agentic artificial intelligence represents an evolving technological paradigm designed to tackle operational hurdles in global crop production. Unlike earlier agricultural software relying on rigid dashboards or isolated machine learning models, agentic systems deploy autonomous entities that receive high-level objectives rather than granular instructions. These systems iteratively gather environmental data, query external tools, generate structured plans, and execute multi-step workflows with minimal human intervention. While artificial intelligence has begun entering agriculture through specialized chatbots and diagnostic models, the review emphasizes that agentic workflows expand these capabilities by coupling reasoning-capable foundation models with structured planning, active environment interaction, and modular tool use across phenomics, crop management, field robotics, and policy. The review traces the technical taxonomy underpinning these systems, delineating the progression from basic autonomous entities to intelligent agents and coordinated multi-agent architectures. In artificial intelligence research, an intelligent agent is formally characterized by three operational hallmarks: reactivity to environmental dynamics, proactivity in pursuing designated objectives, and social capability to communicate and cooperate with other autonomous entities or human managers. While early agent research in the 1990s and 2000s relied on rigid multi-layer frameworks such as Touring Machines and InteRRaP, the integration of large language models provides unprecedented flexibility, contextual comprehension, and dynamic problem-solving capacity. Modern architectures combine these foundation models with retrieval-augmented generation and external memory modules. Retrieval-augmented generation enables models to ground reasoning in external agronomic databases rather than remaining confined to static pre-training weights, while external memory retains critical seasonal context beyond the restrictive boundaries of standard model context windows, facilitating sustained adaptation across changing farm conditions. At their architectural core, agricultural intelligent agents operate within a continuous four-part feedback loop comprising perception, reasoning and decision-making, action, and continuous learning and adaptation. Perception captures ambient conditions through diverse sensory channels, including visual, thermal, olfactory, haptic, and acoustic sensors tailored to specific biological and field tasks. The action component translates computational choices into real-world outcomes, utilizing software application programming interfaces in digital spaces or physical robotic actuators, mobile bases, and end-effectors in field settings. highlights.content: [![GROW YOUR TECH STARTUP](https://sociable.co/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/growyourstartup.png)](https://sociable.co/grow-your-tech-startup) [![GROW YOUR TECH STARTUP](https://sociable.co/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/front-sociable-1.png)](https://sociable.co/grow-your-tech-startup) [Business](https://sociable.co/business/) # How training approaches have shaped the evolution of large language models November 6, 2026 [![](https://sociable.co/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/getty-images-Nu7LYcNFH-4-unsplash.jpg)](https://sociable.co/business/how-training-approaches-have-shaped-the-evolution-of-large-language-models/) ## Act 1: Predict the next token (2018 to 2020) **GPT-1 (2018): the objective works.** [GPT-1](https://cdn.openai.com/research-covers/language-unsupervised/language_understanding_paper.pdf?ref=hackernoon.com) was a 117M-parameter transformer trained on one task: predict the next token in about 7,000 books. To do that well, it had to pick up grammar, facts, and meaning on its own. Fine-tuned on small labeled datasets, it beat purpose-built models on 9 of 12 benchmarks. Next-token prediction turned out to be a way to learn language itself. **GPT-2 (2019): scale, and tasks start to appear.** [GPT-2](https://cdn.openai.com/better-language-models/language_models_are_unsupervised_multitask_learners.pdf?ref=hackernoon.com) grew to 1.5B parameters trained on 40 GB of web text. Without fine-tuning, it began to summarize, translate, and answer questions **zero-shot**. The results were rough, but they hinted that scale alone unlocks new abilities. **GPT-3 (2020): no more fine-tuning.** At 175B parameters, [GPT-3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165?ref=hackernoon.com) could learn a task from a description and a few examples in the prompt, with no weight updates. Using a language model no longer required a labeled dataset, just a good prompt. [Scaling laws](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361?ref=hackernoon.com) showed that bigger models would keep improving predictably. ### The catch Next-token prediction teaches a model what text *looks like*, not how it *should* respond. A pretrained model: * **continues instead of answering.** Ask “How do I bake bread?” and it may write five more questions, because that’s what often follows a question online. * **doesn’t know when to stay quiet.** If it knows how to do something dangerous, nothing in its objective tells it not to say so. * **mirrors the internet**, made-up facts and toxic text included. The capability was there. It just wasn’t pointed anywhere useful. ## Act 2: Be a helpful assistant (2022) The fix was a second training phase: **post-training**. OpenAI’s [InstructGPT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155?ref=hackernoon.com) recipe had three steps: 1. Humans write good example answers, and the model learns to imitate them. 2. Humans rank the model’s answers, and a reward model learns their preferences. 3. The LLM is optimized against that reward model with **reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)**. The effect was dramatic. Raters preferred a 1.3B InstructGPT over the 175B GPT-3. The right objective beat 100x more parameters. In November 2022, OpenAI applied this recipe to a GPT-3.5 model tuned for dialogue and released [ChatGPT](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt/?ref=hackernoon.com). It answered instead of rambling and declined some harmful requests, and it reached an estimated 100 million users in about two months. From here on, the big advances happened *after* pretraining. ## Act 3: Think before you answer (2021 to 2025) **Math and code came first.** From 2021 to 2024, labs pushed hard on both, from [Codex](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.03374?ref=hackernoon.com) to [trained math verifiers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14168?ref=hackernoon.com) to [step-by-step math verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.20050?ref=hackernoon.com). A comprehensive research paper released by Kaspersky demonstrates that probabilistic neural networks cannot reliably distinguish system instructions from unverified data inputs. Security researchers argue that deploying external bolt-on defensive filters fails to mitigate indirect prompt injection or unauthorized tool execution. The investigation outlines an architectural paradigm shift based on Cyber Immunity principles. This methodology enforces hardware-level isolation, deterministic policy monitors, and microkernel sandboxes around non-deterministic reasoning cores. Security specialists published their technical framework in an official [Kaspersky Cyber Immunity research report](https://lp.kaspersky.com/global/ai-agent-cyber-immunity/). Building native resilience directly into the operational fabric prevents compromised agents from hijacking enterprise networks. Modern autonomous agents execute multi-step planning loops, query internal document stores, and invoke arbitrary application programming interfaces across corporate perimeters. When an agent reads unauthenticated emails or parses untrusted web content, embedded adversarial commands can overwrite developer instructions. These instruction poisoning vectors mirror software vulnerabilities exposed in Homeland411’s reporting on [malicious prompt injection and instruction poisoning](https://homeland411.com/hackers-hide-malicious-instructions-ai-coding-projects-hijack-assistants/) in developer ecosystems. Without hardware-enforced compartmentalization, a subverted foundation model inherits all administrative rights allocated to the host application process. **Never Miss An Update**Follow us on Google News to get our latest security, defense and cyber reporting in your feed. Foundation models operate probabilistically. This fundamental reality renders neural weights incapable of acting as their own security reference monitors. Treating the language model as a trusted compute component exposes organizations to catastrophic lateral movement and credential exfiltration. These architectural vulnerabilities parallel real-world intrusions documented in Homeland411’s ongoing analysis of [autonomous agentic exploitation of cloud secrets](https://homeland411.com/microsoft-warns-agentic-ai-weaponized-cloud-secrets/) across corporate infrastructure. Kaspersky proposes applying microkernel isolation models that strictly segregate the model reasoning core from execution tools and data pipelines. By stripping the probabilistic model of direct operating system privileges, security architects eliminate single points of failure across automated workflows. A dedicated, deterministic security monitor intercepts every outbound function call. The monitor enforces immutable access control rules before any network packet transmits. The five dimensions are safety, comfort, efficiency, social interaction and impact on surrounding traffic. Credit: Communications in Transportation Research Self-driving vehicles are moving from pilot projects toward wider commercial deployment, but a vehicle that performs well on conventional tests may still behave in ways that feel hesitant, abrupt or disruptive in real traffic. Researchers at Tongji University have developed a new framework designed to evaluate the overall “intelligence” of high-level autonomous driving systems, rather than judging isolated functions such as braking or lane keeping alone. The study, “Towards the Intelligence Evaluation of High-level Autonomous Vehicles: A Subjective-Objective Mapping Method via LLM,” introduces a Subjective-Objective Mapping Evaluation (SOME) framework. It combines measurable driving data with expert-style assessments generated by a large language model (LLM), then trains an attention-based neural network to learn how objective indicators relate to the broader judgments that human experts make when observing vehicle behavior. The team published their study in [*Communications in Transportation Research*](https://www.sciopen.com/journal/2097-5023) (<https://doi.org/10.26599/COMMTR.2026.9640041>). “A high-level autonomous vehicle should not be evaluated only by whether it avoids a crash,” says Peng Hang, corresponding author of the study and a research professor at Tongji University. “Its behavior should also be judged by whether it moves smoothly, completes tasks efficiently, interacts reasonably with other road users and avoids unnecessarily disrupting surrounding traffic.” **From raw trajectories to expert-like evaluation** The framework evaluates five complementary aspects of autonomous driving behavior: safety, comfort, efficiency, social interaction and impact on surrounding traffic. It uses interaction segments from the Waymo Open Dataset, including following, merging and crossing situations. To improve coverage of rare but important poor-performance cases, the researchers also augmented the dataset with physically feasible low-score interaction samples. In total, the study constructed 5,200 valid interaction segments for training and evaluation. Because language models are not naturally suited to interpreting raw vehicle trajectories and map data, the researchers developed a Data-Language Mapping Module. This component converts key interaction events, vehicle states and abnormal motions into structured natural-language descriptions. highlights.content: [Skip to content](#main-content) [Texas A&M Stories](https://stories.tamu.edu) [View All Stories](/stories/) Share this [Science & Tech](https://stories.tamu.edu/category/science-technology/) # Researchers develop AI tool to improve crisis communication The system filters and categorizes disaster, weather and humanitarian reports to help emergency professionals quickly find relevant information during emergency response. Nov. 6, 2026 By Gabby Shultz, Texas A&M University Division of Marketing and Communications 2 min. read ![A photo of emergency responders in a command center with computer monitors on all of the walls.](https://stories.tamu.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/20241217_Emergency_Operations_Center_Ribbon_Cutting_CS-10-e1793713629856-1408x793.jpg) Texas A&M researchers are developing an AI-based tool to help emergency managers quickly sort through the flood of information that emerges during crises such as hurricanes. Credit: Courtney Sacco/Texas A&M AgriLife During a disaster, emergency managers need quick, reliable data to make decisions, but the vast and changing stream of information that emerges during a crisis can make it difficult to distinguish facts from noise. Researchers from Texas A&M University are working to change that through the development of a tool that uses artificial intelligence to sort through the confusion. Led by postdoctoral researcher Dr. Bo Li, Dr. Ali Mostafavi and Kai Yin in the [Zachry Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering](https://engineering.tamu.edu/civil/index.html), the work uses a large language model to filter the information that emerges during crises such as hurricanes, when emergency officials must make quick decisions while monitoring weather conditions, damage reports, public requests for assistance, search-and-rescue needs and more. In a [recent study on crisis-related social media classification](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1474034626005288), researchers used a benchmark of human-annotated social media posts from multiple disaster events. The model was designed to categorize crisis-related information into three areas: disaster-related, weather-related, and humanitarian information. The model goes even further into classifying each post by event type, informativeness, and humanitarian information type. Li said organizing information in categories could allow emergency personnel to more easily locate details relevant to their needs, such as updates on storm conditions, reports of damage or requests for aid and rescue. The system is under development and has not been deployed during an active disaster. “The team plans to build an AI agent that emergency professionals can talk to when disaster strikes,” Li said. “Ultimately, we want to move from classification toward a more interactive AI system that can better support situational awareness during disasters.” As disasters become more frequent and the amount of available information continues to grow, the researchers say AI-based tools could help response agencies reduce the time spent sorting reports and focus more quickly on decisions that support affected communities. A shipping company adding an agent to dispatch or fleet data must fit current systems, which is taken care of by a [logistics software development company](https://uniquesoftwaredev.com/industries/custom-transportation-software-development/). Shared accounts cause special trouble, since nobody can tell which agent did what. The brief also suggests a small proof of concept, because problems cost far less to fix early. A comprehensive research paper released by Kaspersky demonstrates that probabilistic neural networks cannot reliably distinguish system instructions from unverified data inputs. Security researchers argue that deploying external bolt-on defensive filters fails to mitigate indirect prompt injection or unauthorized tool execution. The investigation outlines an architectural paradigm shift based on Cyber Immunity principles. This methodology enforces hardware-level isolation, deterministic policy monitors, and microkernel sandboxes around non-deterministic reasoning cores. Security specialists published their technical framework in an official [Kaspersky Cyber Immunity research report](https://lp.kaspersky.com/global/ai-agent-cyber-immunity/). Building native resilience directly into the operational fabric prevents compromised agents from hijacking enterprise networks. Modern autonomous agents execute multi-step planning loops, query internal document stores, and invoke arbitrary application programming interfaces across corporate perimeters. When an agent reads unauthenticated emails or parses untrusted web content, embedded adversarial commands can overwrite developer instructions. These instruction poisoning vectors mirror software vulnerabilities exposed in Homeland411’s reporting on [malicious prompt injection and instruction poisoning](https://homeland411.com/hackers-hide-malicious-instructions-ai-coding-projects-hijack-assistants/) in developer ecosystems. Foundation models operate probabilistically. This fundamental reality renders neural weights incapable of acting as their own security reference monitors. Treating the language model as a trusted compute component exposes organizations to catastrophic lateral movement and credential exfiltration. These architectural vulnerabilities parallel real-world intrusions documented in Homeland411’s ongoing analysis of [autonomous agentic exploitation of cloud secrets](https://homeland411.com/microsoft-warns-agentic-ai-weaponized-cloud-secrets/) across corporate infrastructure. LLMs.content: [![GROW YOUR TECH STARTUP](https://sociable.co/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/growyourstartup.png)](https://sociable.co/grow-your-tech-startup) [![GROW YOUR TECH STARTUP](https://sociable.co/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/front-sociable-1.png)](https://sociable.co/grow-your-tech-startup) [Business](https://sociable.co/business/) # How training approaches have shaped the evolution of large language models November 6, 2026 [![](https://sociable.co/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/getty-images-Nu7LYcNFH-4-unsplash.jpg)](https://sociable.co/business/how-training-approaches-have-shaped-the-evolution-of-large-language-models/) ## Act 1: Predict the next token (2018 to 2020) **GPT-1 (2018): the objective works.** [GPT-1](https://cdn.openai.com/research-covers/language-unsupervised/language_understanding_paper.pdf?ref=hackernoon.com) was a 117M-parameter transformer trained on one task: predict the next token in about 7,000 books. To do that well, it had to pick up grammar, facts, and meaning on its own. Fine-tuned on small labeled datasets, it beat purpose-built models on 9 of 12 benchmarks. Next-token prediction turned out to be a way to learn language itself. **GPT-2 (2019): scale, and tasks start to appear.** [GPT-2](https://cdn.openai.com/better-language-models/language_models_are_unsupervised_multitask_learners.pdf?ref=hackernoon.com) grew to 1.5B parameters trained on 40 GB of web text. Without fine-tuning, it began to summarize, translate, and answer questions **zero-shot**. The results were rough, but they hinted that scale alone unlocks new abilities. **GPT-3 (2020): no more fine-tuning.** At 175B parameters, [GPT-3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165?ref=hackernoon.com) could learn a task from a description and a few examples in the prompt, with no weight updates. Using a language model no longer required a labeled dataset, just a good prompt. [Scaling laws](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361?ref=hackernoon.com) showed that bigger models would keep improving predictably. ### The catch Next-token prediction teaches a model what text *looks like*, not how it *should* respond. A pretrained model: * **continues instead of answering.** Ask “How do I bake bread?” and it may write five more questions, because that’s what often follows a question online. * **doesn’t know when to stay quiet.** If it knows how to do something dangerous, nothing in its objective tells it not to say so. * **mirrors the internet**, made-up facts and toxic text included. The capability was there. It just wasn’t pointed anywhere useful. ## Act 2: Be a helpful assistant (2022) The fix was a second training phase: **post-training**. OpenAI’s [InstructGPT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155?ref=hackernoon.com) recipe had three steps: 1. Humans write good example answers, and the model learns to imitate them. 2. Humans rank the model’s answers, and a reward model learns their preferences. 3. The LLM is optimized against that reward model with **reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)**. The effect was dramatic. Raters preferred a 1.3B InstructGPT over the 175B GPT-3. The right objective beat 100x more parameters. In November 2022, OpenAI applied this recipe to a GPT-3.5 model tuned for dialogue and released [ChatGPT](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt/?ref=hackernoon.com). It answered instead of rambling and declined some harmful requests, and it reached an estimated 100 million users in about two months. From here on, the big advances happened *after* pretraining. ## Act 3: Think before you answer (2021 to 2025) **Math and code came first.** From 2021 to 2024, labs pushed hard on both, from [Codex](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.03374?ref=hackernoon.com) to [trained math verifiers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14168?ref=hackernoon.com) to [step-by-step math verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.20050?ref=hackernoon.com). Tsinghua University Press ![Overview of the Subjective-Objective Mapping Evaluation (SOME) framework for high-level autonomous vehicle intelligence.](https://mediasvc.eurekalert.org/Api/v1/Multimedia/9b700144-7158-4e5d-be1c-9fb7e06129d2/Rendition/low-res/Content/Public) **image: The framework converts autonomous-vehicle interaction data into structured language for LLM-based, expert-like assessment, then maps five-dimensional objective metrics to intelligence scores through an attention-based neural network. The five dimensions are safety, comfort, efficiency, social interaction and impact on surrounding traffic.** [view more](/multimedia/1161024) The framework converts autonomous-vehicle interaction data into structured language for LLM-based, expert-like assessment, then maps five-dimensional objective metrics to intelligence scores through an attention-based neural network. The five dimensions are safety, comfort, efficiency, social interaction and impact on surrounding traffic. Credit: Communications in Transportation Research Self-driving vehicles are moving from pilot projects toward wider commercial deployment, but a vehicle that performs well on conventional tests may still behave in ways that feel hesitant, abrupt or disruptive in real traffic. Researchers at Tongji University have developed a new framework designed to evaluate the overall “intelligence” of high-level autonomous driving systems, rather than judging isolated functions such as braking or lane keeping alone. The study, “Towards the Intelligence Evaluation of High-level Autonomous Vehicles: A Subjective-Objective Mapping Method via LLM,” introduces a Subjective-Objective Mapping Evaluation (SOME) framework. It combines measurable driving data with expert-style assessments generated by a large language model (LLM), then trains an attention-based neural network to learn how objective indicators relate to the broader judgments that human experts make when observing vehicle behavior. The team published their study in [*Communications in Transportation Research*](https://www.sciopen.com/journal/2097-5023) (<https://doi.org/10.26599/COMMTR.2026.9640041>). “A high-level autonomous vehicle should not be evaluated only by whether it avoids a crash,” says Peng Hang, corresponding author of the study and a research professor at Tongji University. “Its behavior should also be judged by whether it moves smoothly, completes tasks efficiently, interacts reasonably with other road users and avoids unnecessarily disrupting surrounding traffic.” **From raw trajectories to expert-like evaluation** The framework evaluates five complementary aspects of autonomous driving behavior: safety, comfort, efficiency, social interaction and impact on surrounding traffic. It uses interaction segments from the Waymo Open Dataset, including following, merging and crossing situations. To improve coverage of rare but important poor-performance cases, the researchers also augmented the dataset with physically feasible low-score interaction samples. In total, the study constructed 5,200 valid interaction segments for training and evaluation. Because language models are not naturally suited to interpreting raw vehicle trajectories and map data, the researchers developed a Data-Language Mapping Module. This component converts key interaction events, vehicle states and abnormal motions into structured natural-language descriptions. The descriptions are combined with autonomous-driving knowledge, traffic rules and driving-behavior guidance, enabling the LLM to assess the interaction in an expert-like manner. Nov. 6, 2026 By Gabby Shultz, Texas A&M University Division of Marketing and Communications 2 min. read ![A photo of emergency responders in a command center with computer monitors on all of the walls.](https://stories.tamu.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/20241217_Emergency_Operations_Center_Ribbon_Cutting_CS-10-e1793713629856-1408x793.jpg) Texas A&M researchers are developing an AI-based tool to help emergency managers quickly sort through the flood of information that emerges during crises such as hurricanes. Credit: Courtney Sacco/Texas A&M AgriLife During a disaster, emergency managers need quick, reliable data to make decisions, but the vast and changing stream of information that emerges during a crisis can make it difficult to distinguish facts from noise. Researchers from Texas A&M University are working to change that through the development of a tool that uses artificial intelligence to sort through the confusion. Led by postdoctoral researcher Dr. Bo Li, Dr. Ali Mostafavi and Kai Yin in the [Zachry Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering](https://engineering.tamu.edu/civil/index.html), the work uses a large language model to filter the information that emerges during crises such as hurricanes, when emergency officials must make quick decisions while monitoring weather conditions, damage reports, public requests for assistance, search-and-rescue needs and more. In a [recent study on crisis-related social media classification](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1474034626005288), researchers used a benchmark of human-annotated social media posts from multiple disaster events. The model was designed to categorize crisis-related information into three areas: disaster-related, weather-related, and humanitarian information. The model goes even further into classifying each post by event type, informativeness, and humanitarian information type. Li said organizing information in categories could allow emergency personnel to more easily locate details relevant to their needs, such as updates on storm conditions, reports of damage or requests for aid and rescue. The system is under development and has not been deployed during an active disaster. “The team plans to build an AI agent that emergency professionals can talk to when disaster strikes,” Li said. “Ultimately, we want to move from classification toward a more interactive AI system that can better support situational awareness during disasters.” As disasters become more frequent and the amount of available information continues to grow, the researchers say AI-based tools could help response agencies reduce the time spent sorting reports and focus more quickly on decisions that support affected communities. The conversation spends most of its time on how enterprises actually adopt AI — the split between assistive tools and back-office automation, the token-bill threshold that triggers a switch to open weights, and what still fails — with the "AGI in February 2026" claim appearing only as a brief provocation near the start. Aceituno speaks from the vendor side: StackAI builds workflow automation for enterprises, including defense customers, so his read on model selection comes from watching procurement decisions rather than from benchmark work. Host Sophia frames the discussion around open-source versus closed models and pushes on where enterprises still default to the easiest tool. The reader should come away with a usable mental model of the two enterprise AI adoption paths, the specific conditions that push a company toward open weights, and the open questions around benchmark trust and personalized agents. ## Enterprises adopt AI along two paths, and only one has already flipped to open weights Aceituno separates enterprise AI usage into assistive tools and back-office automation, and says the migration to open-weight models has been far faster in the second category. Assistive deployments — an AI assistant available to employees, such as Copilot Enterprise — still lean on frontier labs, in his account not mainly for the model itself but for the application layer built around it. That is changing as new tooling lets companies run under a model of their own choosing, which matters because a closed model hosted in an unknown cloud and region gives limited visibility into what data it touches, depending on the provider arrangement. The second category, which is StackAI's business, covers processes that persist across the organization, where agents are inserted at points in a workflow or an entire process is converted into agents. Aceituno says the switch to open weights was "very rapid" here because these systems are typically built with custom tooling or AI development platforms that already let the buyer pick the model and control token usage. | Adoption path | Typical deployment | Model preference as of late 2026 | Driver | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Assistive AI | Employee-facing assistant (e.g., Copilot Enterprise) | Frontier closed labs, for the application layer | Ecosystem and ease of use | | Back-office / workflow automation | Agents embedded in persistent organizational processes | Open-weight models | Model choice, token control, residency | The trigger he cites most concretely is cost: enterprises start re-examining their model choice when the annual token bill crosses seven or eight figures. ## The open-versus-closed trade-off has narrowed to governance, not performance Aceituno's core claim is that the old trade-off — good performance from a closed model on a hyperscaler cloud versus full data residency and control in your own data center with an open model — no longer binds for workflow automation. Open Source AI.content: UPDATED 16:27 EST / NOVEMBER 06 2026 ### Thinking Machines debuts Inkling 2 Small amid reported $5B fundraising push Thinking Machines Labs Inc. has released a new large language model that can automate artificial intelligence training tasks. The algorithm, Inkling 2 Small, made its debut late Thursday. Around the same time, Business Insider reported that Thinking Machine is in the process of raising a $5 billion funding round led by Accel. The company, which was founded last year by former OpenAI Group PBC Chief Technology Officer Mira Murati, is expected to receive a $40 billion valuation. Thinking Machines trained Inkling 2 Small on a cluster of GB300 NVL72 racks. Each system contains 72 Blackwell Ultra graphics cards and half as many central processing units. The company completed the initial pre-training phase in 68 hours and subsequently refined the model through a nine-day reinforcement learning workflow. There were also a number of intermediate training steps. Thinking Machines honed Inkling 2 Small’s programming capabilities by giving it hundreds of thousands of long-horizon coding challenges. The task collection included a number of particularly complicated “autoresearch” exercises. They required the model to post-train neural networks, optimize LLM components called kernels and perform other AI research work. Thinking Machines put Inkling 2 Small’s machine learning skills to the test by asking it to fine-tune Qwen3.5-4B. The goal was to improve the open-source LLM’s ability to make predictions such as weather forecasts. According to the company, Inking 2 Small doubled the model’s forecasting score in 4.5 hours. The LLM is also adapt at automating business tasks. It outperformed Spark Open, Kimi K3 and several other open-source models on three popular knowledge work benchmarks. Additionally, it earned higher scores across several financial task datasets. Inkling 2 Small includes a vision encoder that can analyze images. Moreover, it enables the LLM to visually verify the quality of the graphics that it generates. If a user asks the model to create an e-commerce store, it can not only check the website’s code for bugs but also visually inspect product pages to check that they render correctly. The vision encoder accounts for 292 million of Inking 2 Small’s 594 billion parameters. About 17 billion of those parameters activate when a user enters a prompt. Inking 2 Small can adjust the amount of computing power that it spends on tasks, which enables developers to trade off output quality for increased cost-efficiency or vice versa. Particularly savvy users can extend the model’s capabilities by post-training, or customizing it, using their own data. Thinking Machines says that Inkling 2 Small learns faster than its earlier models. That should translate into more cost-efficient post-training runs. Inkling 2 Small is available via Thinking Machines’ Tinker cloud service on launch. Press Send and we'll get you an invite. Mail app didn't open? Copy the message above and send it to . AI News # Qwen 4 Release Date: Is It Out, and Did Alibaba Really Say “Next Week”? By [Lenka Vojtechova](/author/lenka-vojtechova/)  ·  Updated November 6, 2026  ·  14 min read [Qwen](/tag/qwen/)[China](/tag/china/)[LLM](/tag/llm/)[Open-Source Model](/tag/open-source-model/)[Future of AI](/tag/future-of-ai/) ![Thumbnail reading ](/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/qwen-4-hero.webp) Qwen 4 is not out yet. As of **5 November 2026** there is no Qwen 4 model card, download, API name or price. The only thing Alibaba has put in writing is that Qwen 4 **“is currently in training”**. The closest thing to a Qwen 4 release date is one sentence from a conference audience. An attendee at Alibaba Cloud’s Apsara Conference in Amsterdam on **29 October** reported the company’s CTO saying “Qwen4 next week”, which would mean **2 to 8 November**. That week is now half gone, and the claims around it have multiplied. There are four Qwen 4 model names on two stage slides. There are Qwen 4 settings already merged into Alibaba’s own coding tool. And there is an open-weights question that several sites have answered with the wrong model’s news. This guide separates what Alibaba said from what was reported, grades every Qwen 4 rumor, and explains what to use, and what to watch, until Qwen 4 actually ships. This tool, called ARTEX, is an open-source, AI model-driven, autonomous penetration testing framework released on GitHub by a user known as ‘[Autumn-27](https://github.com/AUTUMN-27)’ in July 2026. In October, two threat intelligence companies attributed its use as part of threat actor operations. First, in early October, CrowdStrike linked ARTEX to [a campaign against South Korean financial institutions](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/chinese-hacker-ai-korean-banks/). Infra & Chips.content: ![The Motley Fool](https://g.foolcdn.com/misc-assets/logo-tmf-primary-1-magenta-purple-reversed.svg?_w=320) ![The Motley Fool](https://g.foolcdn.com/image/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fg.foolcdn.com%2Fmisc-assets%2Ftmf_holdingco_logo_stacked_magenta_royalpurple_rev.png&w=96&op=resize) # Dell vs. Nvidia: Chip Stocks Just Suffered Their Worst Sell-Off Since 2020. Which Is the Better Buy for 2027? Dell's cash flow and NVIDIA's margins tell very different stories, and a sizable valuation gap may matter more than either name suggests. ## Key Points The [artificial intelligence (AI)](https://www.fool.com/investing/stock-market/market-sectors/information-technology/ai-stocks/) boom has fueled extraordinary growth across the technology sector, but a recent sell-off has Wall Street questioning whether massive infrastructure investments can continue to justify elevated valuations. For investors looking toward 2027, the pullback presents an opportunity to reassess two major beneficiaries of the AI boom: **Dell Technologies**([DELL](/quote/nyse/dell/) +3.67%) and **Nvidia** ([NVDA](/quote/nasdaq/nvda/) +2.77%). Dell provides the servers and infrastructure needed to support AI workloads, while Nvidia designs the advanced chips powering them. Both have benefited from surging demand, but their business models, profitability, and valuations differ substantially. As investors become more selective about AI exposure, those differences could determine which stock offers the more compelling long-term opportunity. ## The case for Dell Technologies Dell provides servers, storage systems, and personal computers to enterprises, governments, and cloud providers. Its Infrastructure Solutions Group has become an increasingly important driver of growth as demand for AI-optimized servers accelerates. In fiscal 2026, Dell generated $113.5 billion in revenue, an increase of approximately 19% year over year. Net income reached $5.9 billion, representing a profit margin of 5.2%. More recent results highlight the momentum behind its AI business. In the second quarter of fiscal 2027, revenue surged 58% to $47 billion, with AI-optimized server revenue doubling to $16.4 billion. Dell also reported a $95 billion AI server backlog, providing considerable visibility into future demand, although orders remain subject to customer spending decisions. At the end of fiscal 2026, its debt-to-equity ratio was negative due to a shareholder equity deficit, while its current ratio stood near 0.9x. Nevertheless, the company generated substantial operating cash flow, providing resources to fund operations and return capital to shareholders. ## The case for NVIDIA NVIDIA is a leader in [semiconductor stocks](https://www.fool.com/investing/stock-market/market-sectors/information-technology/semiconductor-stocks/), supplying the GPUs, networking equipment, and software infrastructure powering much of the industry's expansion. In fiscal 2026, Nvidia generated $215.9 billion in revenue, an increase of approximately 65% year over year. Net income reached $120.1 billion, representing an exceptional profit margin of 55.6%. Infra & Chips.content: TAIPEI, Nov 6 (Reuters) - A global race to build AI infrastructure is unleashing billions of dollars of investment in advanced chip packaging, a once unglamorous aspect of technology that has become a critical bottleneck in turning out the world's most powerful processors. As demand for artificial intelligence chips outstrips available packaging capacity, companies from ​Nvidia (NVDA.O) and AMD (AMD.O) to lesser-known players in Taiwan are expanding production, while equipment makers develop new tools, interviews with more than a dozen industry executives and analysts show. "Packaging was always that thing that ‌you just didn't worry about," former Intel chief executive Pat Gelsinger, now a partner at Playground Global, told reporters in Taipei recently. Advanced packaging could eventually account for as much as half the value of a chip product, Gelsinger estimated, as some of today's graphics and central processing units can integrate 10 or more chips, sometimes as many as 20. Revenue from advanced packaging is forecast to overtake that earned via the traditional route for the first time in 2026, says research firm Yole Group, with capital spending on the technology expected to near $28 ​billion. ## TAIWAN FIRM DOMINATES CHIP-ON-WAFER SUBSTRATE The world's largest contract chipmaker, Taiwan's TSMC (2330.TW), dominates the most sophisticated advanced packaging technology, including chip-on-wafer-on-substrate, or CoWoS. The technology links separate pieces of silicon, such as processors and memory chips, on a shared ​base, to let them work together at high speed. It is widely used by Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom (AVGO.O), as well as cloud companies developing their own AI chips. But TSMC's capacity ⁠limits have spurred some chip designers to seek additional supply. Nvidia, for example, is providing billions of dollars in financing to expand CoWoS packaging capacity at Siliconware Precision Industries, or SPIL, a unit of Taiwan's ASE Technology (3711.TW), said an industry ​executive familiar with the matter, who sought anonymity for lack of authorisation to talk to media. The funding will support new factory space and equipment, the executive said. The scale of the support has not previously been reported. Nvidia did not respond ​to a request for comment. ASE said it does not comment on market rumours involving its customers. ## A FUNDAMENTAL CHIPMAKING SHIFT The scramble to invest reflects a broader change in manufacturing of powerful chips, as more chip designers use advanced packaging to integrate multiple chips, such as processors and memory, into a single package. That allows the ensemble to work together faster as one system, in contrast with the practice of decades, when packaging served mainly to protect chips and provide the electrical connections to attach them to circuit boards. The shift comes as it ​become harder and costlier to win performance gains by shrinking and adding transistors, the tiny switches inside a chip. The newer packaging technique is especially important for AI chips, which need to shuffle vast amounts of data between processors and ​nearby memory. Speeding up such transfers hastens the process of training and running AI models. ## A RACE FOR TSMC ALTERNATIVES TSMC's tight capacity offers an opportunity for smaller suppliers, such as Taiwan's Powertech Technology (6239.TW). "Everyone is looking for a solution outside TSMC," its chairman, D K ‌Tsai, told reporters ⁠in August. "They don't want to rely entirely on TSMC."
